claim: ATM deficiency led to the 11q23 chromosome translocation, the most frequent chromosome abnormalities in secondary leukemia.
source: Previously, we showed that ATM deficiency led to the 11q23 chromosome translocation, the most frequent chromosome abnormalities in secondary leukemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: ARP8, a subunit of the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex, is phosphorylated after etoposide treatment.
source: Here, we show that ARP8, a subunit of the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex, is phosphorylated after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 is regulated by ATM and ATR.
source: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 is regulated by ATM and ATR, and attenuates its interaction with INO80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 attenuates its interaction with INO80.
source: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 is regulated by ATM and ATR, and attenuates its interaction with INO80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ATM-regulated phosphorylation of ARP8 reduces the excessive loading of INO80 onto the breakpoint cluster region.
source: The ATM-regulated phosphorylation of ARP8 reduces the excessive loading of INO80 and RAD51 onto the breakpoint cluster region.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ATM-regulated phosphorylation of ARP8 reduces the excessive loading of RAD51 onto the breakpoint cluster region.
source: The ATM-regulated phosphorylation of ARP8 reduces the excessive loading of INO80 and RAD51 onto the breakpoint cluster region.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8, regulated by ATM, plays an important role in maintaining the fidelity of DNA repair to prevent the etoposide-induced 11q23 abnormalities.
source: These findings suggest that the phosphorylation of ARP8, regulated by ATM, plays an important role in maintaining the fidelity of DNA repair to prevent the etoposide-induced 11q23 abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and represents the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Chromosome translocations are one of the most common types of genetic rearrangements induced by DNA damaging agents, such as ionizing radiation and certain chemotherapies.
source: Chromosome translocations are one of the most common types of genetic rearrangements induced by DNA damaging agents, such as ionizing radiation and certain chemotherapies.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about chromosome translocations.

claim: The presence of disease-specific chromosome translocations, especially in hematological malignancies such as the t(9;22) or Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myelocytic leukemia, has been reported.
source: The presence of disease-specific chromosome translocations, especially in hematological malignancies such as the t(9;22) or Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myelocytic leukemia, has been reported.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about disease-specific chromosome translocations.

claim: Molecular studies of the breakpoints of disease-specific chromosome translocations have revealed the clustering of the breakpoints in specific regions, designated as the breakpoint cluster region (BCR).
source: Molecular studies of the breakpoints of such disease-specific chromosome translocations have revealed the clustering of the breakpoints in specific regions, designated as the breakpoint cluster region (BCR).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about breakpoint cluster regions.

claim: In lymphoid malignancies, the involvement of the physiological recombination of immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor genes in chromosome translocations has been suggested, due to the presence of signal sequences for the recombination at the breakpoints.
source: In lymphoid malignancies, the involvement of the physiological recombination of immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor genes in chromosome translocations has been suggested, due to the presence of signal sequences for the recombination at the breakpoints.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about lymphoid malignancies.

claim: Chromosome translocations arise as a consequence of errors in the repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs).
source: Chromosome translocations arise as a consequence of errors in the repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the origin of chromosome translocations.

claim: Eukaryotic cells utilize a variety of repair pathways for DSBs, including two major ones, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination repair (HR).
source: Eukaryotic cells utilize a variety of repair pathways for DSBs, including two major ones, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination repair (HR).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about DNA repair pathways.

claim: In the absence of canonical DSB repair pathways, the activation of the alternative NHEJ (Alt-EJ) pathway and the inactivation of DNA polymerase theta are implicated in chromosomal translocations.
source: In the absence of these canonical pathways, the activation of the alternative NHEJ (Alt-EJ) pathway and the inactivation of DNA polymerase theta are implicated in chromosomal translocations (Zelensky et al., 2017) (Mizuno et al., 2009; Ruiz et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HR is regarded as a precise DSB repair system, since either the intact sister chromatid or the homologous region is used as the template for repair.
source: In contrast, HR is regarded as a precise DSB repair system, since either the intact sister chromatid or the homologous region is used as the template for repair.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about homologous recombination.

claim: Both the depletion and overexpression of the RAD51 recombinase lead to chromosomal abnormalities.
source: However, both the depletion and overexpression of the RAD51 recombinase, a key factor involved in HR, lead to chromosomal abnormalities (Reliene et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The precise regulation of the recombination activity is required for DNA repair to prevent chromosome translocations.
source: Therefore, the precise regulation of the recombination activity is also required for DNA repair to prevent chromosome translocations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the previous statement about RAD51 depletion and overexpression.

claim: DNA damage leads to the activation of the DNA damage response and repair pathways.
source: DNA damage leads to the activation of the DNA damage response and repair pathways.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about DNA damage response.

claim: The ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein regulates the DNA damage response in reaction to DSBs, through its kinase activity.
source: The ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein regulates the DNA damage response in reaction to DSBs, through its kinase activity (Clouaire et al., 2017; Guleria and Chandna, 2016; Shiloh, 2003; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alterations in the function of ATM play pathologic roles in the development of leukemia/lymphoma and cancer.
source: Alterations in the function of ATM play pathologic roles in the development of leukemia/lymphoma and cancer (Khanna, 2000; Oguchi et al., 2003; Reliene et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromosome translocations involving the MLL gene on 11q23 are the most frequent chromosome abnormalities in secondary leukemia associated with chemotherapy employing etoposide, a topoisomerase II poison.
source: Chromosome translocations involving the MLL gene on 11q23 are the most frequent chromosome abnormalities in secondary leukemia associated with chemotherapy employing etoposide, a topoisomerase II poison.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about secondary leukemia.

claim: An increase of 11q23 translocations is observed in the ATM kinase activity-deficient fibroblast cell line AT5BIVA.
source: An increase of 11q23 translocations is observed in the ATM kinase activity-deficient fibroblast cell line AT5BIVA (Nakada et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A deficiency of ATM led to the excessive binding of RAD51 and the chromatin remodeling factor INO80 to the BCR in the MLL gene after etoposide treatment.
source: We showed previously that a deficiency of ATM, a DNA damage signaling kinase, led to the excessive binding of RAD51 and the chromatin remodeling factor INO80 to the BCR in the MLL gene after etoposide treatment (Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: INO80 is conserved in eukaryotes and acts as an integral scaffold for assembling other proteins into the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex.
source: INO80 is conserved in eukaryotes and acts as an integral scaffold for assembling other proteins into the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex (Chen et al., 2011; Morrison et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for transcription.
source: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for transcription (Lafon et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2015), replication (Falbo and Shen, 2012; Vassileva et al., 2014) and DNA repair (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gospodinov et al., 2011; Morrison et al., 2004; Seeber et al., 2013; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for replication.
source: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for transcription (Lafon et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2015), replication (Falbo and Shen, 2012; Vassileva et al., 2014) and DNA repair (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gospodinov et al., 2011; Morrison et al., 2004; Seeber et al., 2013; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for DNA repair.
source: The INO80 complex plays an important role in chromatin reorganization for transcription (Lafon et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2015), replication (Falbo and Shen, 2012; Vassileva et al., 2014) and DNA repair (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gospodinov et al., 2011; Morrison et al., 2004; Seeber et al., 2013; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The INO80 complex is required for effective DNA end resection at the early stage of HR in budding yeast and human cells.
source: The INO80 complex is required for effective DNA end resection at the early stage of HR in budding yeast and human cells (Gospodinov et al., 2011; Lademann et al., 2017; Tsukuda et al., 2005; Tsukuda et al., 2009; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The decreased fidelity of DNA repair by the inappropriate regulation of HR repair in ATM-deficient cells could lead to chromosomal translocations.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the decreased fidelity of DNA repair by the inappropriate regulation of HR repair in ATM-deficient cells could lead to chromosomal translocations.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' speculation based on previous findings.

claim: INO80 forms a chromatin remodeling complex with more than 15 subunits.
source: INO80 forms a chromatin remodeling complex with more than 15 subunits (Jin et al., 2005; Shen et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARP8 functions as a nucleosome recognition module and enhances the nucleosome-binding affinity of the INO80 protein complex.
source: Among the subunits of the INO80 complex, ARP8 functions as a nucleosome recognition module and enhances the nucleosome-binding affinity of the protein complex (Saravanan et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARP8 is required for the binding of INO80 and RAD51 to the BCR in the MLL gene after etoposide treatment.
source: In this study, we found that ARP8 is required for the binding of INO80 and RAD51 to the BCR in the MLL gene after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The DNA damage-dependent phosphorylation of ARP8 is regulated by ATM and ATR after etoposide treatment.
source: We also showed that the DNA damage-dependent phosphorylation of ARP8 is regulated by ATM and ATR after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The ATM-dependent phosphorylation of ARP8 negatively regulates the interaction between INO80 and ARP8, leading to the reduced binding of INO80 and RAD51 to the BCR after etoposide treatment.
source: The ATM-dependent phosphorylation of ARP8 negatively regulates the interaction between INO80 and ARP8, leading to the reduced binding of INO80 and RAD51 to the BCR after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: ATR was not involved in the regulation of the etoposide-induced binding of RAD51 to the BCR.
source: In contrast, ATR was not involved in the regulation of the etoposide-induced binding of RAD51 to the BCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ATM plays distinct roles from ATR in the phosphorylation of ARP8 to prevent the etoposide-induced 11q23 chromosome translocations, through the negative regulation of INO80 and RAD51 binding to the BCR.
source: These findings suggest that ATM plays distinct roles from ATR in the phosphorylation of ARP8 to prevent the etoposide-induced 11q23 chromosome translocations, through the negative regulation of INO80 and RAD51 binding to the BCR.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' interpretation of their findings and is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The substrates of ATM contain the core sequence with an SQ or TQ motif.
source: The substrates of ATM contain the core sequence with an SQ or TQ motif (Kim et al., 1999; Matsuoka et al., 2007; O'Neill et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARP8 has an SQ motif at S412 and Q413.
source: By searching for SQ or TQ motifs in the subunits of the INO80 complex, we found that APR8 had an SQ motif at S412 and Q413.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The SQ motif in ARP8 is indicated as a putative phosphorylation site in the PhosphoSitePlus database.
source: This motif in ARP8 is indicated as a putative phosphorylation site in the PhosphoSitePlus database (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a database.

claim: ARP8 is required for DNA binding by INO80 in yeast and mammals.
source: ARP8 is required for DNA binding by INO80 in yeast and mammals, and the ARP8 knockout in human cells impairs the binding of INO80 to chromatin and causes defects in DNA repair (Kashiwaba et al., 2010; Saravanan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ARP8 knockout in human cells impairs the binding of INO80 to chromatin and causes defects in DNA repair.
source: ARP8 is required for DNA binding by INO80 in yeast and mammals, and the ARP8 knockout in human cells impairs the binding of INO80 to chromatin and causes defects in DNA repair (Kashiwaba et al., 2010; Saravanan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The level of ARP8 phosphorylation was significantly increased from 2 hr after etoposide treatment.
source: The immunoblotting analysis, using antibodies against the ATM/ATR substrate, revealed that the level of ARP8 phosphorylation was significantly increased from 2 hr after etoposide treatment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The disappearance of the signal by a protein phosphatase treatment validated that the derived signal resulted from the phosphorylation of ARP8.
source: The disappearance of the signal by a protein phosphatase treatment validated that the derived signal resulted from the phosphorylation of ARP8 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ser412 is the sole site within ARP8 that is phosphorylated in response to etoposide treatment.
source: An immunoprecipitation analysis revealed that the etoposide-induced phosphorylation was completely abolished by the S412A substitution, indicating that Ser412 is the sole site within ARP8 that is phosphorylated in response to etoposide treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The etoposide-induced ARP8 phosphorylation in BIVA cells was lower than that in 11–4 cells.
source: An immunoblotting analysis revealed that the etoposide-induced ARP8 phosphorylation in BIVA cells was lower than that in 11–4 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8 in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells after etoposide treatment was repressed by the ATM-specific inhibitor, KU55933 (ATMi).
source: Moreover, the phosphorylation of ARP8 in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells after etoposide treatment was repressed by the ATM-specific inhibitor, KU55933 (ATMi) (Figure 1E; lanes 1–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ATM regulates the ARP8 phosphorylation after etoposide treatment.
source: These findings suggest that ATM regulates the ARP8 phosphorylation after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: ATMi did not completely abolish the etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8.
source: Since ATMi did not completely abolish the etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8, we next examined the relevance of ATR, another PI3-family kinase member sharing the same phosphorylation motif with ATM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ATR is responsible for the phosphorylation in the DNA replication stress response, and is activated by ATM after ionizing radiation.
source: ATR is responsible for the phosphorylation in the DNA replication stress response, and is activated by ATM after ionizing radiation (Cuadrado et al., 2006; Jazayeri et al., 2006; Myers and Cortez, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 was strongly repressed by the ATR inhibitor VE821 (ATRi) in 11–4 cells.
source: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 was strongly repressed by the ATR inhibitor VE821 (ATRi) in 11–4 cells (Figure 1E, lanes 9–12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ATR is the major kinase responsible for etoposide-induced ARP8 phosphorylation.
source: This finding suggests that ATR is the major kinase responsible for etoposide-induced ARP8 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Casein kinase 2 was not involved in the phosphorylation of ARP8 after etoposide treatment.
source: In contrast, casein kinase 2, another kinase involved in the DNA damage response (Olsen et al., 2012) (Guerra et al., 2014) was not involved in the phosphorylation of ARP8 after etoposide treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8 at S412 after etoposide treatment is regulated by ATM and ATR.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the phosphorylation of ARP8 at S412 after etoposide treatment is regulated by ATM and ATR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The enrichment of γH2AX on BCR was observed in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells after etoposide treatment.
source: The enrichment of γH2AX on BCR was observed in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells after etoposide treatment, suggesting that etoposide induces DNA damage specifically at the BCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Etoposide induces DNA damage specifically at the BCR.
source: The enrichment of γH2AX on BCR was observed in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells after etoposide treatment, suggesting that etoposide induces DNA damage specifically at the BCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The depletion of ARP8 reduced the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment in BIVA cells.
source: A chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis revealed that the depletion of ARP8 reduced the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment in BIVA cells ((Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ARP8 is required for loading INO80 onto the MLL BCR after etoposide treatment in BIVA cells.
source: Since the depletion of ARP8 did not affect the levels of INO80 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), the result suggests that ARP8 is required for loading INO80 onto the MLL BCR after etoposide treatment in BIVA cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: The expression of the S412A mutant in ATM-proficient cells increased the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment.
source: The ChIP analysis revealed that the expression of the S412A mutant in ATM-proficient cells increased the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ATMi treatment increased the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment in ATM-proficient cells expressing wild-type ARP8.
source: Moreover, ATMi treatment increased the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment in ATM-proficient cells expressing wild-type ARP8 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 represses the binding of INO80 to the BCR.
source: These findings suggest that the etoposide-induced phosphorylation of ARP8 represses the binding of INO80 to the BCR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The ATMi treatment failed to enhance the enrichment of INO80 at the BCR in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells expressing the ARP8 S412A mutant.
source: Importantly, the ATMi treatment failed to enhance the enrichment of INO80 at the BCR in ATM-proficient 11–4 cells expressing the ARP8 S412A mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ARP8 phosphorylation at S412 regulated by ATM is responsible for the excessive binding of INO80 at the BCR after etoposide treatment.
source: This suggests that ARP8 phosphorylation at S412 regulated by ATM is responsible for the excessive binding of INO80 at the BCR after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression of the phosphomimetic mutant S412D in BIVA cells reduced the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment.
source: Consistently, the expression of the phosphomimetic mutant S412D in BIVA cells reduced the binding of INO80 to the BCR after etoposide treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8 represses the loading of INO80 onto the MLL BCR in response to etoposide-induced damage.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the phosphorylation of ARP8 represses the loading of INO80 onto the MLL BCR in response to etoposide-induced damage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: Etoposide treatment increased the interaction between INO80 and ARP8 in the ATM-proficient U2OS cells.
source: We found that etoposide treatment increased the interaction between INO80 and ARP8 in the ATM-proficient U2OS cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The etoposide-induced interaction between INO80 and ARP8 was enhanced by the treatment of U2OS cells with an ATM inhibitor.
source: The etoposide-induced interaction between INO80 and ARP8 was enhanced by the treatment of U2OS cells with an ATM inhibitor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATM negatively regulates the interaction of ARP8 with INO80 after etoposide treatment.
source: These findings raised the possibility that ATM negatively regulates the interaction of ARP8 with INO80 after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An increased level of interaction of the ARP8 S412A mutant with INO80 after etoposide treatment was observed, as compared to that of wild-type ARP8 (ARP8 WT) in ATM-proficient cells.
source: An immunoprecipitation analysis showed an increased level of interaction of the ARP8 S412A mutant with INO80 after etoposide treatment, as compared to that of wild-type ARP8 (ARP8 WT) in ATM-proficient cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8 represses its interaction with INO80 after etoposide treatment.
source: These findings support the notion that the phosphorylation of ARP8 represses its interaction with INO80 after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: An immunoprecipitation analysis revealed the increased interaction of INO80 with ARP8 WT, but not with the S412D mutant, in ATM-deficient BIVA cells after etoposide treatment.
source: An immunoprecipitation analysis revealed the increased interaction of INO80 with ARP8 WT, but not with the S412D mutant, in ATM-deficient BIVA cells after etoposide treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A proximity ligation assay confirmed the decreased interaction of INO80 with the ARP8 S412D mutant.
source: A proximity ligation assay confirmed the decreased interaction of INO80 with the ARP8 S412D mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In yeast, INO80 promotes DNA end resection and RAD51 binding to ssDNA for homology search/invasion during HR.
source: In yeast, INO80 promotes DNA end resection and RAD51 binding to ssDNA for homology search/invasion during HR (Lademann et al., 2017; Tsukuda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The depletion of INO80 by siRNA reduced the loading of RAD51 onto the MLL BCR in BIVA cells after etoposide treatment.
source: A ChIP assay revealed that the depletion of INO80 by siRNA reduced the loading of RAD51 onto the MLL BCR in BIVA cells after etoposide treatment, suggesting that human INO80 promotes RAD51 binding to the BCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Human INO80 promotes RAD51 binding to the BCR.
source: A ChIP assay revealed that the depletion of INO80 by siRNA reduced the loading of RAD51 onto the MLL BCR in BIVA cells after etoposide treatment, suggesting that human INO80 promotes RAD51 binding to the BCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The depletion of ARP8 reduced the binding of RAD51 to the MLL BCR in BIVA cells after etoposide treatment.
source: A ChIP analysis showed that the depletion of ARP8 reduced the binding of RAD51 to the MLL BCR in BIVA cells after etoposide treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ARP8 is involved in the excessive binding of RAD51 to the BCR in BIVA cells.
source: Since the depletion of ARP8 did not affect the level of RAD51 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), these findings suggest the involvement of ARP8 in the excessive binding of RAD51 to the BCR in BIVA cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of the ARP8 phosphorylation-deficient mutant S412A increased the RAD51 binding to the BCR of the MLL gene after etoposide treatment in ATM-proficient cells.
source: The expression of the ARP8 phosphorylation-deficient mutant S412A increased the RAD51 binding to the BCR of the MLL gene after etoposide treatment in ATM-proficient cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In ATM-proficient cells, ATMi treatment resulted in an increase of RAD51 binding to the BCR.
source: In ATM-proficient cells, ATMi treatment resulted in an increase of RAD51 binding to the BCR (Figure 4B), but it did not cause a further increase of RAD51 when ARP8 S412A was expressed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATMi treatment did not cause a further increase of RAD51 binding to the BCR when ARP8 S412A was expressed.
source: In ATM-proficient cells, ATMi treatment resulted in an increase of RAD51 binding to the BCR (Figure 4B), but it did not cause a further increase of RAD51 when ARP8 S412A was expressed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression of the ARP8 phosphomimetic mutant S412D in ATM-deficient BIVA cells repressed the excessive binding of RAD51 to the BCR.
source: In contrast, the expression of the ARP8 phosphomimetic mutant S412D in ATM-deficient BIVA cells repressed the excessive binding of RAD51 to the BCR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ARP8 phosphorylation at S412 represses the loading of RAD51 onto the MLL BCR after etoposide treatment.
source: These results strongly suggest that ARP8 phosphorylation at S412 represses the loading of RAD51 onto the MLL BCR after etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, and 4D.

claim: The phosphorylation of ARP8 regulated by ATM may negatively regulate the loading of RAD51 onto the BCR after etoposide treatment, by repressing the loading of the INO80 complex.
source: Taken together, the phosphorylation of ARP8 regulated by ATM may negatively regulate the loading of RAD51 onto the BCR after etoposide treatment, by repressing the loading of the INO80 complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The number of BIVA cells carrying split FISH signals after etoposide treatment was significantly reduced by the siRNA-mediated depletion of ARP8.
source: A two-color fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis, covering the upstream and downstream regions of the MLL BCR, revealed that the number of BIVA cells carrying split FISH signals after etoposide treatment was significantly reduced by the siRNA-mediated depletion of ARP8, suggesting the involvement of ARP8 in 11q23 chromosomal abnormalities in ATM-deficient cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: ARP8 is involved in 11q23 chromosomal abnormalities in ATM-deficient cells.
source: A two-color fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis, covering the upstream and downstream regions of the MLL BCR, revealed that the number of BIVA cells carrying split FISH signals after etoposide treatment was significantly reduced by the siRNA-mediated depletion of ARP8, suggesting the involvement of ARP8 in 11q23 chromosomal abnormalities in ATM-deficient cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The number of split signal positive cells among the ATM-proficient 11–4 cells was increased by the depletion of ARP8.
source: In contrast, the number of split signal positive cells among the ATM-proficient 11–4 cells was increased by the depletion of ARP8 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ATM prevents the etoposide-induced 11q23 chromosome translocations through the regulation of ARP8.
source: These findings suggest that ATM prevents the etoposide-induced 11q23 chromosome translocations through the regulation of ARP8.
